name: Acne Vulgaris
symptoms: Blackheads and whiteheads
Red, painful bumps (papules & pustules)
Deep, painful lumps (nodules & cysts)
Oily skin and scarring
causes: Excessive sebum (oil) production
Follicular hyperkeratinization (clogging)
Bacterial colonization by C. acnes
Inflammation
diagnosis: Visual skin examination by a dermatologist evaluating grade of acne and oil glands activity.
treatment: Topical retinoids, salicylic/benzoyl peroxide washes, oral antibiotics, or low-dose oral isotretinoin. Clinical peeling and blue light therapy can speed up clearance.
prevention: Wash face twice daily with a gentle, pH-balanced cleanser
Avoid touching or picking active lesions
Use non-comedogenic makeup and skincare
Maintain a low-glycemic index diet
doctorAdvice: Do not squeeze or pop pimples. It forces infection deeper, causing permanent scarring and hyperpigmentation that takes months to treat.

name: Androgenetic Alopecia (Pattern Hair Loss)
symptoms: Receding hairline (especially in men)
Thinning hair at the crown or vertex
Widening of the middle part (in women)
Finer, shorter hair shafts over time
causes: Genetics (family history of baldness)
Sensitivity of hair follicles to Dihydrotestosterone (DHT)
Microinflammation around the follicle
diagnosis: Scalp trichoscopy mapping hairline, checking for follicular miniaturization and single-hair units.
treatment: Topical minoxidil, oral DHT blockers (finasteride), growth factor therapy, scalp microneedling, or hair transplant surgery.
prevention: Eat a protein-rich, nutrient-dense diet
Manage stress through exercise or meditation
Avoid tight hairstyles that cause traction on hair roots
Avoid applying harsh chemicals directly to the scalp
doctorAdvice: Pattern hair loss is progressive. The earlier you start medical therapy to block DHT and stimulate the root, the more hair you can preserve.

name: Atopic Dermatitis (Eczema)
symptoms: Severe, unbearable itching
Dry, red, rough, or cracked skin patches
Small fluid-filled blisters that crust over
Thickened, leathery skin from scratching
causes: Genetic mutations in the filaggrin gene (compromises skin barrier)
Immune system hypersensitivity
Environmental triggers
riskFactors: Personal or family history of asthma, hay fever, or allergies
Living in cold or highly polluted environments
diagnosis: Clinical examination of skin barrier integrity, distribution of rash, and allergen history.
treatment: Intensive ceramide-dominant moisturizers, topical steroids or steroid-free immunomodulators, and biologics (dupilumab) for severe cases.
prevention: Moisturize skin within 3 minutes after bathing
Use lukewarm water instead of hot water for showers
Wear loose, breathable cotton clothing
Avoid fragrances, parabens, and harsh detergents
doctorAdvice: Scratching worsens the rash and introduces bacterial infections. Apply a cold compress or a ceramide cream immediately to quiet the itch reflex.

name: Psoriasis
symptoms: Red patches of skin covered with silvery scales
Dry, cracked skin that may itch or bleed
Thickened, pitted, or yellowing nails
Stiff, painful joints
causes: Autoimmune condition accelerating skin cell growth cycle
T-cells attacking healthy skin cells mistakenly
diagnosis: Visual mapping of plaques, nail checks, joint examination, and skin biopsy to exclude other conditions.
treatment: Topical coal tar, vitamin D analogues, topical steroids, phototherapy, or oral systemic immunosuppressants and targeted biologics.
prevention: Keep skin moisturized to prevent plaque cracking
Minimize stress and trigger factors
Limit alcohol intake and stop smoking
Get moderate, safe sun exposure
doctorAdvice: Psoriasis is not just a skin disease; it is a systemic inflammatory condition. Managing diet, stress, and systemic inflammation is vital for long-term clearance.

name: Melasma
symptoms: Symmetrical gray-brown patches on cheeks
Dark pigmentation on the forehead and bridge of nose
Pigment patches on the upper lip and chin
causes: Overproduction of melanin by hyperactive melanocytes
Hormonal stimulation of pigment cells
UV and heat triggers
riskFactors: Oral contraceptive pills or hormone therapies
diagnosis: Wood's Lamp exam and dermoscopic inspection to assess if melasma is epidermal, dermal, or mixed.
treatment: Triple combination creams (Kligman's), tranexamic acid, chemical peels (glycolic/retinol), or low-fluence Q-switched lasers.
prevention: Wear broad-spectrum sunscreen SPF 50+ indoors and outdoors
Reapply sunscreen every 2-3 hours when outdoors
Wear wide-brimmed hats and sunglasses
Avoid hot environments, steam baths, and kitchen heat when possible
doctorAdvice: Melasma is highly sensitive. Harsh treatments can cause rebound hyperpigmentation. A gentle approach combined with constant sunscreen is the safest way to manage it.

name: Rosacea
symptoms: Persistent facial redness, especially cheeks and nose
Visible broken blood vessels (telangiectasia)
Small red, pus-filled bumps (resembling acne)
Burning or stinging sensation in the eyes
causes: Vascular hyperreactivity
Demodex folliculorum mites on skin
Environmental and neurovascular triggers
Genetics
riskFactors: Frequent consumption of spicy foods, alcohol, or hot beverages
Extreme temperature changes and wind exposure
diagnosis: Clinical observation of facial flushing patterns and ruling out acne or lupus.
treatment: Topical metronidazole, ivermectin cream, oral doxycycline, and vascular lasers (IPB/pulse dye) to target broken capillaries.
prevention: Identify and avoid dietary triggers (spicy food, caffeine, alcohol)
Use physical (mineral) sunscreens rather than chemical ones
Wash face with very gentle cleansers
Protect face from cold winds and extreme heat
doctorAdvice: Rosacea skin is extremely reactive. Avoid harsh physical scrubs, toners containing alcohol, and foaming cleansers which strip the barrier.

name: Vitiligo
symptoms: Depigmented (chalky white) skin patches
Loss of color in tissues inside the mouth and nose
Premature graying of scalp hair, eyebrows, or beard
causes: Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes
Oxidative stress leading to melanocyte self-destruction
Genetic susceptibility
diagnosis: Wood's Lamp exam showing bright white fluorescence, blood panels checking thyroid antibodies.
treatment: Topical calcineurin inhibitors, topical steroids, narrow-band UVB phototherapy, excimer laser, or melanocyte transplant surgery for stable patches.
prevention: Protect white patches from sunburn using high SPF sunscreen
Avoid skin trauma (cuts, friction, tight clothing) which can trigger new patches (Koebner phenomenon)
doctorAdvice: Stable vitiligo can be successfully repigmented surgically. If your white patches have not changed size for over a year, you are a candidate for melanocyte transplant.

name: Tinea (Fungal Ringworm Infection)
symptoms: Itchy, red, circular rash with elevated borders
Scaling, cracking, or peeling skin
Bald patches on the scalp with broken hair
Nail thickening and discoloration
causes: Dermatophyte fungal infection feeding on skin keratin
Spreading via direct contact or damp environments
diagnosis: Clinical appearance, KOH mount microscopy of skin scrapings showing fungal hyphae.
treatment: Oral and topical antifungal medicines (terbinafine, itraconazole, luliconazole) taken for a minimum of 4 weeks.
prevention: Keep skin clean and dry, especially body folds
Change socks and underwear daily
Wear loose cotton clothes
Never use OTC creams without consulting a doctor
doctorAdvice: Avoid 'triple-action' creams from pharmacies. They contain strong steroids that temporarily mask the itch but feed the fungus, leading to chronic resistant infections.

name: Contact Dermatitis (Skin Allergies)
symptoms: Red, itchy rash localized to area of contact
Dry, cracked, scaly skin
Blisters, swelling, or burning sensation
causes: Skin contact with an allergen or irritant, triggering immune response
riskFactors: Frequent use of cosmetics, hair dyes, or artificial jewelry
Occupations involving wet work, cleaning, or chemicals
diagnosis: Patch testing using common allergen grids left on the back for 48-72 hours.
treatment: Identifying and avoiding the allergen, topical steroid creams, oral antihistamines, and barrier moisturizers.
prevention: Use fragrance-free, hypoallergenic products
Wear gloves when handling cleaning chemicals
Test new cosmetics on the inner arm before applying to the face
doctorAdvice: If you develop rashes after using hair dye, jewelry, or perfumes, have a patch test done to identify the exact chemical (e.g., Nickel, PPD) so you can avoid it.

name: Urticaria (Hives)
symptoms: Raised, red, or skin-colored itchy welts (wheals)
Welts that move, fade, and reappear elsewhere within hours
Swelling of the face, lips, or eyelids (angioedema)
causes: Histamine release by mast cells in the skin
Allergic reaction, viral infections, physical triggers, or autoantibodies
riskFactors: Known allergies to food or medications
diagnosis: Clinical presentation, checking for dermographism, blood panels, and allergen testing if chronic.
treatment: Non-sedative oral antihistamines, avoiding triggers, and biologic therapy (Omalizumab) for chronic hives.
prevention: Avoid known triggers (certain foods, NSAID painkillers)
Wear loose-fitting clothes to prevent skin friction
Avoid hot baths during a hives outbreak
doctorAdvice: A single welt of hives should disappear within 24 hours without scarring. If it stays longer or leaves bruising, it could indicate urticarial vasculitis and needs biopsy.

name: Seborrheic Dermatitis
symptoms: Yellowish, greasy scales on the scalp
Itchy, white flakes (dandruff)
Redness and scaling on eyebrows, nose sides, and chest
Oily scalp with a burning itch
causes: Inflammatory response to Malassezia yeast on the oily parts of skin
Excess sebum production
diagnosis: Clinical examination of scalp scale distribution.
treatment: Antifungal shampoos (ketoconazole, zinc pyrithione), topical anti-inflammatory lotions, and regular scalp clarifying routines.
prevention: Wash hair regularly with a medicated shampoo
Avoid heavy oils and hair gels on the scalp
Eat a balanced diet low in sugar and yeast
doctorAdvice: Applying heavy mustard or coconut oil to a dandruff-prone scalp feeds the Malassezia yeast, worsening the scales and itching. Use water-based serums instead.

name: Warts
symptoms: Rough, grainy bumps on fingers or hands
Fleshy, flat growths on the face or neck
Painful, hard growths on the soles of feet (plantar warts)
causes: Infection of the upper skin layer by Human Papillomavirus (HPV)
riskFactors: Walking barefoot in public showers or pool decks
diagnosis: Visual inspection by a skin specialist.
treatment: Radiofrequency ablation, cryotherapy (freezing), or topical salicylic acid paints.
prevention: Do not touch or scratch another person's warts
Wear footwear in public locker rooms and showers
Keep hands and feet clean and dry
doctorAdvice: Warts are viral and can spread rapidly across your body or to family members. Get them removed early while they are small to prevent spreading.

name: Moles (Nevi)
symptoms: Small, brown or black spots on the skin
Flat or raised circular growths
Constant color and borders (benign moles)
causes: Clusters of melanocyte pigment cells growing together
diagnosis: Dermoscopy evaluating ABCD guidelines (Asymmetry, Border, Color, Diameter).
treatment: None needed for benign moles. Aesthetic removal via radiofrequency ablation or surgical shave.
prevention: Perform monthly skin self-exams for new or changing spots
Apply broad-spectrum sunscreen daily
Avoid tanning beds
doctorAdvice: Keep an eye on the ABCDEs of moles. If a mole becomes asymmetric, has irregular borders, changes color, grows larger than 6mm, or bleeds, seek a dermatology check immediately.

name: Keloids & Hypertrophic Scars
symptoms: Thick, raised, firm scar tissue growing beyond the original injury site
Itchy or tender skin growth
Red, purple, or dark brown scar coloration
causes: Overproduction of collagen during skin healing after injury
riskFactors: Injuries on chest, shoulders, or earlobes
diagnosis: Clinical inspection of scar margins.
treatment: Intralesional steroid injections, silicone gel sheeting, laser therapy, or cryotherapy.
prevention: Avoid body piercings or elective skin surgeries if prone to keloids
Apply silicone sheets immediately after surgical incisions heal
Avoid picking at acne or skin scabs
doctorAdvice: Never surgically cut a keloid without additional treatments (like steroid shots). Cutting alone has a 50-80% recurrence rate, often returning larger.

name: Xerosis (Dry Skin)
symptoms: Tightness, especially after bathing
Rough, flaky, or peeling skin texture
Fine lines, cracks, or itchy skin
Redness in severe cases
causes: Loss of natural moisturizing factors (NMFs) and lipids in the stratum corneum
Environmental humidity drop
riskFactors: Frequent use of hot water and foaming soaps
diagnosis: Visual exam of skin moisture levels.
treatment: Thick moisturizers containing urea, ceramides, or hyaluronic acid, combined with mild cleansers.
prevention: Moisturize skin immediately after washing
Use a humidifier in dry indoor environments
Drink plenty of water and limit hot showers to 5-10 minutes
doctorAdvice: Dry skin is vulnerable to eczema and infections because the barrier is cracked. Switch to cream-based body washes and moisturize daily.

name: Onychomycosis (Fungal Nail Infection)
symptoms: Thickened, yellow-brown nail plate
Brittle, crumbly, or ragged nail edges
Distorted nail shape
Nail separating from the nail bed (onycholysis)
causes: Fungal invasion of the nail bed, often starting from athlete's foot
riskFactors: Age, poor blood circulation, or diabetes
diagnosis: KOH preparation of nail clippings and clinical examination.
treatment: Oral antifungal tablets, topical nail lacquers, or laser nail therapy.
prevention: Keep feet clean and dry, especially between toes
Clip nails straight across and sanitize nail clippers
Wear moisture-wicking socks and breathable shoes
doctorAdvice: Fungal nail infections do not resolve on their own. Because nails grow slowly, oral therapies or special medicated lacquers must be used for several months.

name: Stretch Marks (Striae)
symptoms: Parallel indented lines on skin
Red or purple lines (striae rubrae) that fade to silvery-white (striae albae)
Thin, glossy skin texture over marks
causes: Rapid stretching of the skin rupturing collagen and elastin in the dermis
riskFactors: Rapid weight gain or muscle growth
Prolonged use of topical steroid creams
diagnosis: Clinical examination of scar stages (red vs. white).
treatment: Fractional lasers, microneedling RF, or prescription retinoid creams (effective for early red stretch marks).
prevention: Keep skin moisturized during pregnancy or weight shifts
Maintain steady weight gain/loss goals
doctorAdvice: Stretch marks are easiest to treat when they are still red or purple. Once they turn silvery-white, they are much harder to remodel.

name: Hirsutism (Excessive Hair)
symptoms: Thick, dark hair growth in androgen-sensitive zones (face, chest, back)
Acne, oily skin, or hair thinning on scalp
causes: Increased levels of male hormones (androgens) or high sensitivity of hair follicles to normal hormone levels
diagnosis: Hormone level panels, pelvic ultrasound (for PCOS), and hair growth pattern staging.
treatment: Oral anti-androgen medicines, lifestyle modification, and laser hair removal.
prevention: Manage PCOS through diet, exercise, and medical supervision
doctorAdvice: For excessive facial hair, medical evaluation is key. Combining laser hair removal with hormonal management yields the best results.

name: Herpes Zoster (Shingles)
symptoms: Pain, burning, or tingling in a band-like pattern on one side of the body
Red rash appearing a few days after the pain
Fluid-filled blisters that break open and crust over
Extreme sensitivity to touch
causes: Reactivation of the Varicella-Zoster virus (chickenpox virus) dormant in nerve tissue
riskFactors: Weakened immune system or high stress
diagnosis: Clinical presentation of unilateral dermatomal rash, or PCR check of blister fluid.
treatment: Antiviral tablets (acyclovir, valacyclovir) taken within 72 hours of rash onset, pain management.
prevention: Shingles vaccine for adults over 50
Managing stress and maintaining immune health
doctorAdvice: Antivirals must be started within 72 hours of the rash appearing to prevent a painful long-term nerve condition called Postherpetic Neuralgia.

name: Milia
symptoms: Tiny, dome-shaped white or yellow bumps on cheeks, nose, or eyelids
Firm, hard bumps that do not squeeze out like blackheads
causes: Keratin trapped under the skin surface due to dead skin buildup or skin damage
riskFactors: Skin trauma (blisters, burns, or sun damage)
diagnosis: Clinical examination.
treatment: Sterile extraction (using a fine needle to express the cyst), chemical peels, or radiofrequency ablation.
prevention: Exfoliate regularly with mild AHA/BHA chemical exfoliants
Avoid heavy oils and petroleum-based moisturizers on the face
doctorAdvice: Milia are small cysts. Squeezing them at home will only bruise the skin and cause scarring. They need a tiny, sterile prick for safe extraction.
